title: Hydrocarbons
objectives: Describe the unreactivity of alkanes and their complete and incomplete combustion
Describe the free-radical substitution of alkanes by chlorine or bromine in UV light, including initiation, propagation and termination
Describe the cracking of larger alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes
Describe the addition reactions of alkenes with H₂, steam, hydrogen halides and halogens, and their oxidation by cold dilute and hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄
Describe the mechanism of electrophilic addition, including the use of the inductive effect to explain the stability of carbocations and the major product (Markovnikov addition)
Use the reactions of alkenes with KMnO₄ to deduce the position of C=C bonds
prior: σ and π bonds, sp² and sp³ (Chapter 3 and 13)
why: Alkanes are our main fuels and the raw materials for plastics; alkenes from cracking are the starting point for most of the organic chemicals industry. This chapter introduces the first two mechanisms you must draw, free-radical substitution and electrophilic addition, which are examined every year in Paper 2.
intro: Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) contain only strong, non-polar C–C and C–H σ bonds, so they are unreactive except with oxygen and with halogens in UV light. Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) contain a C=C with an electron-rich π bond, which attracts electrophiles and makes alkenes much more reactive.

blocks.h: Alkanes are unreactive because C–C and C–H bonds are strong and almost non-polar: there is nothing to attract nucleophiles or electrophiles.

items: Incomplete (limited O₂): produces toxic CO and soot (C). C₈H₁₈ + 8½O₂ → 8CO + 9H₂O
Engines also form NO (from N₂ + O₂) and release unburnt hydrocarbons (Chapter 12).

blocks.h: With Cl₂ or Br₂ in ultraviolet light, H atoms are replaced by halogen atoms. Overall: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.

head: stage
equation
what happens
rows: UV light causes homolytic fission of the weak Cl–Cl bond

CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl
CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
a radical reacts and a new radical forms: a chain reaction

blocks.name: radical
blocks.title: Radical step sorter
blocks.h: Classify each step as initiation, propagation or termination.
The reaction is hard to control: further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄, and longer alkanes give mixtures of isomers. Termination can join two alkyl radicals into a longer alkane.

Long-chain alkanes are broken into shorter alkanes and alkenes by heating (about 500 °C with a zeolite or Al₂O₃ catalyst, or higher without). For example C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄. Shorter alkanes are more useful as fuels; alkenes are used to make polymers and other chemicals.

blocks.name: alkenerx
blocks.title: Alkene reaction explorer
blocks.h: Choose an alkene and a reagent to see the product, the conditions and the type of reaction, including which product is major.

items: H–Br is polar: H δ+, Br δ−. A curly arrow goes from the C=C π bond to the δ+ H, and another from the H–Br bond to Br.
A curly arrow from a lone pair on Br⁻ to the C⁺ forms the C–Br bond.

blocks.h: With Br₂, the electron-rich C=C induces a dipole in the Br–Br bond; the δ+ Br acts as the electrophile in the same way.

Alkyl groups push electrons towards a positive carbon (positive inductive effect), so carbocation stability is tertiary > secondary > primary. The major product forms via the more stable carbocation: H adds to the carbon of the C=C that already has more H atoms (Markovnikov addition).

blocks.q: Give the major product of HBr with 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, and explain.
steps: H can add to C3, leaving a tertiary carbocation on C2
or to C2, leaving a secondary carbocation on C3
the tertiary carbocation is more stable (three alkyl groups)
blocks.err: Putting Br on the carbon that had more hydrogens.

blocks.wrong: In electrophilic addition, Br⁻ attacks first.
blocks.right: The electrophile (δ+ H or δ+ Br) is attacked first by the π electrons. Br⁻ only bonds once the carbocation has formed.

head: conditions
what happens
example: propene
rows: two OH groups add across the C=C: a diol; purple → colourless

blocks.cap: What each carbon of the C=C becomes with hot concentrated KMnO₄
head: carbon of the C=C carries
becomes
rows: one H and one alkyl group (=CHR)

blocks.h: Working backwards from the products tells you where the C=C was. A ring alkene gives one product with a group at each end.

blocks.q: An alkene C₆H₁₂ gives propanone and propanoic acid with hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄. Identify the alkene.
steps: propanoic acid CH₃CH₂COOH came from a =CHCH₂CH₃ end
join the two ends with a C=C
blocks.err: Forgetting that the acid carbon was the C=C carbon itself.

summary: Alkanes are unreactive: strong, non-polar C–C and C–H bonds.
Complete combustion → CO₂ + H₂O; incomplete → CO and C.
Free-radical substitution (UV light): initiation (X₂ → 2X•), propagation (two steps), termination (two radicals join).
Cracking: long alkane → shorter alkane + alkene (heat, zeolite catalyst).
Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition with H₂ (Ni), steam (H₃PO₄), HX and X₂.
Bromine water: orange → colourless with C=C.
Carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary (positive inductive effect); the major product comes from the more stable carbocation.
Cold dilute acidified KMnO₄ → diol. Hot concentrated → C=C broken: =CH₂ → CO₂; =CHR → RCOOH; =CR₂ → ketone.

flash.a: Strong C–C and C–H bonds; almost non-polar

flash.q: Two propagation steps for CH₄ + Cl₂?
flash.a: CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃• + HCl; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•
About 500 °C with a zeolite (or Al₂O₃) catalyst

flash.q: Conditions for hydrogenation of an alkene?
Why are tertiary carbocations most stable?
flash.a: Three alkyl groups donate electron density (positive inductive effect)

flash.q: Product of cold dilute KMnO₄ with ethene?
Product of =CH₂ with hot conc. KMnO₄?
Product of =CR₂ with hot conc. KMnO₄?

practice.q: Write the initiation, two propagation and two termination steps for the reaction of ethane with bromine in UV light.
practice.a: Br₂ → 2Br•; C₂H₆ + Br• → C₂H₅• + HBr; C₂H₅• + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + Br•; termination e.g. C₂H₅• + Br• → C₂H₅Br and 2C₂H₅• → C₄H₁₀

practice.q: Write an equation for cracking dodecane, C₁₂H₂₆, into octane and an alkene.
Describe the mechanism for the reaction of HBr with propene and explain why 2-bromopropane is the major product.
practice.a: π electrons attack δ+ H of HBr; H–Br bond breaks to Br⁻; secondary carbocation CH₃C⁺HCH₃ (more stable than primary); Br⁻ attacks C⁺. Two alkyl groups stabilise the secondary carbocation.

practice.q: An alkene gives butanone and CO₂ with hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄. Identify it.
Give the product of cold dilute acidified KMnO₄ with but-2-ene and what is seen.
Why does the reaction of methane with chlorine give a mixture of products?
practice.a: Cl• can attack CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, etc. (further substitution), and termination steps give other products such as ethane.

assessment_s.q:
Propene is made by cracking and used to make other chemicals.
(a) Write an equation for cracking hexane to form propene and one other product. [1]
(b) Give the reagents and conditions, and name the major product, for the reaction of propene with steam. [3]
(c) Explain why the product in (b) is the major one. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) C₆H₁₄ → C₃H₆ + C₃H₈
(b) steam, H₃PO₄ catalyst, about 300 °C and 6 MPa; propan-2-ol
(c) H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end, forming the secondary carbocation, which is more stable than the primary one because of the electron-donating alkyl groups

assessment_s.q:
Alkene A, C₅H₁₀, reacts with hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄ to give propanone and ethanoic acid.
(a) Identify A and name it. [2]
(b) Give the product of A with cold dilute acidified KMnO₄ and state what you would see. [2]
(c) A reacts with HBr. Name the major product. [1]

pp.skill: Type of reaction and by-product of alkane halogenation
pp.stem: Methane and bromine are mixed in ultraviolet light. Which describes the reaction?
pp.exp: CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr. A Br atom replaces an H atom; the H leaves as HBr.

pp.skill: The role of UV light
pp.stem: Ethane reacts with bromine in ultraviolet light. What does the light do?
pp.exp: Initiation: Br₂ → 2Br• by homolytic fission. The Br–Br bond is weak enough for UV to break it; C–H is not broken by the light.

pp.skill: Classifying steps in a radical mechanism
pp.mis: Calling any step that makes a product termination
pp.stem:
Two steps in the reaction of ethane with chlorine:
step 1: Cl₂ → 2Cl•
step 2: C₂H₅• + C₂H₅• → C₄H₁₀
Which is correct?
pp.exp: Initiation makes radicals from a molecule. Termination joins two radicals to make a molecule, removing radicals.

pp.skill: A product formed only by termination
pp.mis: Choosing HCl, which comes from propagation
pp.stem: Ethane and chlorine react in UV light. Which product can only be formed by a termination step?
pp.exp: Two ethyl radicals combine: 2C₂H₅• → C₄H₁₀. HCl forms in propagation (Cl• + C₂H₆ → C₂H₅• + HCl). H₂ and C₂H₄ are not formed.

pp.skill: Possible products of a radical reaction
pp.stem:
Methane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Which could be products?
1 ethane
2 hydrogen
3 dichloromethane
pp.exp: Ethane: termination (2CH₃• → C₂H₆). CH₂Cl₂: further substitution of CH₃Cl. H• radicals are not formed, so no H₂.

pp.skill: A possible termination product
pp.mis: Choosing a fragment that needs a C–C bond to break
pp.stem: Propane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Which could be formed in a termination step?
pp.exp: Two propyl radicals join: 2C₃H₇• → C₆H₁₄ (hexane or 2,3-dimethylbutane, depending on which radicals). No C–C bonds break, so no CH₄.

pp.skill: Counting different first propagation steps
pp.stem: In the first propagation step, Cl• removes an H atom from the alkane. How many different first propagation steps are possible for 2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CH?
pp.exp: There are two kinds of H: the nine on CH₃ groups (giving (CH₃)₂CHCH₂•) and the one on the central C (giving (CH₃)₃C•).

pp.skill: Counting monochloro products including optical isomers
pp.stem: Pentane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Counting optical isomers separately, how many monochloro products, C₅H₁₁Cl, can form?
pp.exp: 1-chloropentane, 3-chloropentane, and 2-chloropentane, which is chiral (two optical isomers): 4.

pp.skill: An alkane that gives only one monochloro product
pp.stem: Which isomer of C₅H₁₂ forms only one monochloroalkane with chlorine in UV light?
pp.exp: In C(CH₃)₄ all twelve H atoms are equivalent, so only (CH₃)₃CCH₂Cl forms.

pp.skill: Possible products of cracking
pp.stem:
Decane, C₁₀H₂₂, is cracked. Which could be found in the products?
1 C₂H₄
2 C₈H₁₈
3 C₉H₂₀
pp.exp: C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄ balances. C₉H₂₀ would leave CH₂, which is not a stable product. Cracking gives a smaller alkane and an alkene.

pp.skill: Classifying hydrogenation
pp.stem: Propene reacts with hydrogen over a nickel catalyst to form propane. What type of reaction is this?
pp.exp: Two molecules form one. (It is also a reduction, but that is not an option.)

pp.skill: Mechanism of HBr addition
pp.stem: What is the mechanism of the reaction of hydrogen bromide with but-2-ene?
pp.exp: The electron-rich π bond attacks the δ+ H of HBr (the electrophile), then Br⁻ adds to the carbocation.

pp.skill: The intermediate in electrophilic addition
pp.stem: Bromine adds to propene in the dark. Which describes the organic intermediate?
opts: It is a negatively charged ion.
It is a carbocation with a positive charge.
pp.exp: The π electrons attack the δ+ Br of the polarised Br₂, forming a C–Br bond and a carbocation; Br⁻ then attacks the C⁺.

pp.skill: Bromine water with a saturated hydrocarbon
pp.stem: Bromine water is added to cyclohexane in the dark and shaken. What is seen?
pp.exp: Cyclohexane has no C=C, so no addition takes place. (Cyclohexene would decolourise the bromine water.)

pp.skill: Product of adding bromine to a C₄H₈ alkene
pp.stem: Which compound can be made by adding Br₂ to an alkene of formula C₄H₈?
pp.exp: Addition puts one Br on each carbon of the C=C, so the two Br atoms must be on adjacent carbons: but-2-ene + Br₂ → 2,3-dibromobutane.

pp.skill: The most stable carbocation
pp.stem: Which carbocation forms in the greatest amount when HBr adds to 2-methylpropene?
pp.exp: H adds to the CH₂ end, giving the tertiary carbocation, stabilised by three electron-donating alkyl groups.

pp.skill: Order of carbocation stability
pp.stem: Which shows carbocations in order of increasing stability?
pp.exp: Each alkyl group pushes electron density towards C⁺ (positive inductive effect): tertiary > secondary > primary.

pp.skill: Major product of HCl addition (Markovnikov)
pp.mis: Putting Cl on the carbon with more H
pp.stem: What is the major product when 2-methylbut-1-ene reacts with HCl?
pp.exp: H adds to CH₂=, giving the tertiary carbocation (CH₃)C⁺(C₂H₅)CH₃; Cl⁻ then bonds there.

pp.skill: Naming the major addition product
pp.stem: What is the systematic name of the major product of HBr with 3-methylpent-2-ene, CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
pp.exp: H adds to C2 (the CH), forming the tertiary carbocation at C3; Br bonds to C3.

pp.skill: Addition of an interhalogen compound
pp.mis: Adding the less electronegative atom to the wrong carbon
pp.stem: Iodine monobromide, IBr, adds to propene in the same way as HBr. Which product forms in the greatest amount?
pp.exp: I is the δ+ end (less electronegative) and acts like H⁺: it adds to the CH₂ end, giving the secondary carbocation. Br⁻ adds to the middle carbon.

pp.skill: Stereoisomers of an addition product
pp.stem: The major product of HBr with 3-methylbut-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH(CH₃)₂, is 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (ignoring rearrangement). How many stereoisomers does this product have?
pp.exp: C2 carries H, Br, CH₃ and CH(CH₃)₂: one chiral centre, so two optical isomers (formed as a racemic mixture).

pp.skill: Which hydrocarbon undergoes both radical and electrophilic reactions
pp.stem: Which hydrocarbon can undergo both free-radical substitution and electrophilic addition?
pp.exp: Propene has a C=C for addition and C–H bonds on its CH₃ group that can be substituted by radicals in UV light.

pp.skill: Products of cold and hot KMnO₄ with an alkene
pp.mis: Forgetting that diols and acids both react with Na
pp.stem: Pent-2-ene reacts with cold dilute acidified KMnO₄ to give X, and with hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄ to give a mixture Y. Which statement is correct?
opts: X and Y both react with 2,4-DNPH.
Neither X nor Y reacts with sodium.
X reacts with NaHCO₃ to give CO₂.
X and Y both react with sodium.
pp.exp: X is pentane-2,3-diol (OH groups react with Na). Y is ethanoic acid + propanoic acid (react with Na, and with NaHCO₃). Neither contains C=O that reacts with 2,4-DNPH.

pp.skill: Comparing the products of cold and hot KMnO₄
pp.mis: Expecting a carboxylic acid from a fully substituted alkene
pp.stem: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene reacts with cold dilute acidified KMnO₄ to give X, and with hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄ to give Y. Which statement is correct?
opts: X and Y both react with sodium.
X is oxidised by acidified dichromate(VI).
pp.exp: X is (CH₃)₂C(OH)C(OH)(CH₃)₂, a tertiary diol (not oxidised, no C=O). Y is propanone (a ketone: orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH; no reaction with Na or NaOH).

pp.skill: Deducing an alkene from its oxidation product
pp.mis: Not realising each carbon of the C=C carries two alkyl groups
pp.stem: An alkene reacts with hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄. Propanone is the only organic product. What is the alkene?
pp.exp: (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂ splits into two (CH₃)₂C=O. A gives propanone + ethanoic acid; B gives propanone + CO₂; D gives ethanoic acid.

pp.skill: Identifying a gaseous alkene from its density and oxidation
pp.mis: Not using M = density × molar volume
pp.stem: Gaseous hydrocarbon Z has a density of 2.33 × 10⁻³ g cm⁻³ at room conditions. With hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄ it gives only one organic product, a carboxylic acid. What is Z?
pp.exp: M = 2.33 × 10⁻³ × 24 000 = 56: C₄H₈. CH₃CH=CHCH₃ → 2CH₃COOH only. But-1-ene gives propanoic acid + CO₂; methylpropene gives propanone + CO₂.

pp.skill: Ring alkene with cold and hot KMnO₄
pp.mis: Expecting the ring to stay intact with hot KMnO₄
pp.stem: Cyclopentene reacts with acidified KMnO₄. Which row gives the products?
opts: cold dilute: cyclopentane-1,2-diol; hot concentrated: HOOC(CH₂)₃COOH
cold dilute: cyclopentanone; hot concentrated: cyclopentane-1,2-diol
cold dilute: cyclopentane-1,2-diol; hot concentrated: cyclopentanone
cold dilute: HOOC(CH₂)₃COOH; hot concentrated: CO₂ only
pp.exp: Cold: two OH groups add across the C=C. Hot: the C=C is broken; each former C=C carbon (each with one H) becomes COOH, opening the ring to pentanedioic acid.

pp.skill: Oxidative cleavage of a ring alkene with a methyl group
pp.mis: Making two separate products from a ring
pp.stem: What is the product when 1-methylcyclohexene reacts with hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄?
pp.exp: The ring opens at the C=C. The carbon with CH₃ becomes a ketone C=O; the carbon with H becomes COOH. One molecule: 6-oxoheptanoic acid.

pp.skill: Products of hot KMnO₄ with a terminal alkene
pp.stem: What are the products when pent-1-ene reacts with hot concentrated acidified KMnO₄?
pp.exp: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH=CH₂: the =CHR end gives butanoic acid; the =CH₂ end is oxidised all the way to CO₂ (and H₂O).

pp.skill: Number of C=C bonds from the volume of hydrogen
pp.mis: Using 24 cm³ instead of 24 000 cm³ per mole
pp.stem: 0.020 mol of hydrocarbon X reacts completely with 960 cm³ of hydrogen at room conditions to form an alkane. What could X be?
pp.exp: n(H₂) = 960/24 000 = 0.040 mol: 2 mol H₂ per mol of X, so X has two C=C bonds.

pp.skill: Steps to convert an alkene into a ketone
pp.mis: Using hot KMnO₄, which breaks the chain
pp.stem: Which steps convert propene into propanone?
opts: steam with an H₃PO₄ catalyst, then heat under reflux with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
H₂ with Ni, then acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
pp.exp: Hydration gives mainly propan-2-ol (Markovnikov); oxidising a secondary alcohol gives propanone. Hot KMnO₄ splits the molecule; C stops at the alcohol; D gives propane, which does not oxidise.

pp.skill: Following hydration then oxidation
pp.stem: But-1-ene reacts with steam (H₃PO₄ catalyst). The major product is heated under reflux with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. What is the final organic product?
pp.exp: Hydration gives mainly butan-2-ol (OH on the more substituted carbon). Oxidising a secondary alcohol gives a ketone: butanone.

pp.skill: Cracking, the bromine test and electrophilic addition
pp.stem: Alkenes are made by cracking long-chain alkanes from crude oil.

parts.q: State the conditions for catalytic cracking, and write an equation for cracking decane into octane and one other product.
ms: high temperature (about 500 °C) with a zeolite / Al₂O₃ catalyst (or very high temperature without catalyst)
C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄

parts.q: State what is seen when aqueous bromine is shaken with pent-1-ene, and name the product formed with Br₂.
ms: orange to colourless
1,2-dibromopentane

parts.q: Describe the mechanism for the reaction of HBr with but-2-ene, including curly arrows and the intermediate.
ms: H–Br polar (δ+ H, δ− Br); curly arrow from C=C π bond to H
curly arrow from H–Br bond to Br, forming Br⁻
carbocation intermediate CH₃CH₂C⁺HCH₃
curly arrow from a lone pair on Br⁻ to C⁺, giving 2-bromobutane

parts.q: 2-methylbut-2-ene reacts with HCl to give two products. Explain which is the major product.
ms: 2-chloro-2-methylbutane is major
it forms via the more stable tertiary carbocation (more electron-donating alkyl groups) rather than the secondary one

pp.skill: Free-radical substitution: steps and products
pp.stem: Butane reacts with chlorine in ultraviolet light. Products include 1-chlorobutane, 2-chlorobutane and octane.

parts.q: State what is meant by a free radical, and name the type of bond fission that forms Cl• from Cl₂.
ms: a species with an unpaired electron
homolytic fission

parts.q: Write two propagation steps that convert butane into 2-chlorobutane.
ms: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃CH•CH₂CH₃ + HCl
CH₃CH•CH₂CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃ + Cl•

parts.q: Write a termination step that forms octane.
ms: 2CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂• → CH₃(CH₂)₆CH₃

parts.q: Suggest why the products contain more 2-chlorobutane than the 4 : 6 ratio of secondary to primary H atoms would suggest.
ms: the secondary radical is more stable (more alkyl groups donating electron density), so it forms faster

pp.skill: Electrophilic addition of bromine
pp.stem: Bromine reacts with propene in an organic solvent at room temperature.

ms: two reactant molecules combine to form a single product

parts.q: Explain how the non-polar Br₂ molecule can act as an electrophile.
ms: the electron-rich C=C repels electrons in Br₂, inducing a dipole (δ+ Br nearer the C=C)

parts.q: Describe the mechanism, including the intermediate and the product.
ms: curly arrow from C=C to the δ+ Br
curly arrow from Br–Br bond to the δ− Br, forming Br⁻
carbocation intermediate (secondary: CH₃C⁺HCH₂Br)
Br⁻ attacks C⁺ with a curly arrow from its lone pair: 1,2-dibromopropane
